title: How many of you are making D&D-style games? I’m building one too.
author: No-Fruit7735
selftext:
Just saw a D&D-style text-based game here and realized I’m building something pretty similar.

Mine has a defined beginning and ending, but everything in between is true free-roam. The story is generated from scratch based on your actions and their consequences, rather than following prewritten branches.

Minigames are text-based too — it’s not a traditional graphical RPG.

What’s the standout part of yours?

comments.author: Charming_You_25
comments.body:
So basically ai dungeon without a starting point?

I’m also building something ai dm adjacent that’s text based. My approach is that the llm is a renderer for player created worlds that answers the question “can they do this”. Your approach is quicker to start but i think you will discover llms are not good writers with no sense of pacing or how difficult / easy things should be and you’ll end up in a slopquest.

There’s quite a few of us building ai dnd inspired games, but most people are cagy about it. It’s its still a large untapped market. you’ll start getting ads from the people who launched first (and are still early) i expect. 

I encourage you to keep building! It seems most people aren’t using the right memory architecture and won’t be able to scale. Solve that and a few tests:  
\-Have npc secrets the llm doesn’t know about and cannot leak (llms love to leak anything they know).  
\-Npc’s do things off screen.  
\-Item permanence and nesting. It’s boring if players can invent things at will “i pull out my gun and shoot it”. Also can you find a buried treasure chest and loot the items inside  
\-A player walks into a bar, the bartender is cold to the stranger, then hears how they saved the town and warms towards them.

replies.author: No-Fruit7735
replies.body:
Yes, exactly — you’re seeing the same problems I ran into.

I ended up building a separate memory architecture and a Game Master engine that controls the actual world state. I use two LLMs: one primarily makes decisions, while the other handles the narrative/rendering side.

Most of the lore, major NPCs, and the overall act structure exist before the game starts. But the acts are only milestones, not scripted sequences. There are 12 acts in the current story, and there can be many completely different paths between those milestones.

I’ve been testing this specifically because I really don’t want the LLM constantly pushing the player toward the finale. So far it works pretty well. You can pursue the main objective, wander around, search for another way out, talk to people, build relationships, investigate random things, etc. The player doesn’t have to “advance the plot” every few turns. That freedom is basically the main thing I’ve been trying to solve.

Unimportant NPCs can also be created dynamically, including their background/history when needed, but the system decides what information should actually be available to the LLM/player instead of just dumping everything into context. That was important because otherwise LLMs tend to invent things or accidentally reveal information they shouldn’t know.

And surprisingly it’s pretty cheap. Around 30 turns in Act 0 currently costs me roughly $0.06 total.

I also made the story system modular, so theoretically you can define your own beginning, ending, lore and milestone structure and run it through the same engine rather than having the entire game hardcoded around one campaign.

I’ve looked at quite a few of the other AI-DnD / AI-RPG projects too, and I agree about the “slopquest” problem. A lot of them gradually turn into the same kind of generated quest loop.

There’s another thing I’ve noticed though: some projects claim to have a fully AI-driven game engine, but the responses come back extremely fast. Either they’re burning a ridiculous amount of money on very fast models, somehow getting them essentially free, or a lot more of the story is predefined/scripted than the developers themselves realize. Sometimes it feels like the AI is mostly selecting or rewriting prepared content rather than actually simulating the world.

The tests you mentioned — hidden NPC information, off-screen NPC actions, item permanence/nesting, and reputation changing future interactions — are pretty much exactly the kind of tests I think separate an actual AI game world from a chatbot telling an adventure story.

comments.author: ericoinen
comments.body: ours goes the other way on one thing: the model narrates but never rolls. a plain rules engine owns every die, HP, item and grid position, and the LLM only gets told what happened. how do you keep consequences consistent when the story is generated from scratch?

replies.author: No-Fruit7735
replies.body:
I handle that mostly through milestones. The world can go in completely spontaneous directions, but the GM tries to bend whatever is currently happening toward the next milestone instead of forcing a specific scene.

It took me about a month to tune that balance. For example, if a milestone requires a dragon fight but the player decided to go on a date instead, the system might decide the dragon attacks during the date. So the milestone still happens, but through the direction the player chose rather than pulling them out of it.

That example isn’t actually in my game, but that’s basically the idea. Otherwise the model can easily turn into an infinite life sim and forget there was ever a larger story.

replies.author: ericoinen
replies.body: the dragon showing up at the date is a good way to put it. bending toward the milestone instead of cutting to it probably also means the player never notices there was a plan
